Abstract—The advancement of Internet technology has spurred
a rise in the dissemination of misinformation, which has had pro-
foundly negative impacts across a wide array of ﬁelds. To address
this issue, the ﬁeld of Misinformation Detection (MD), which fo-
cuses on the automated identiﬁcation of online misinformation,
has gained signiﬁcant traction among researchers. In our study, we
introduce an innovative plug-and-play augmentation technique for
MD, termed DEtecting Misinformation by Uncovering Common-
sense Conﬂict (DEMUC). Our approach is grounded in previous psy-
chological research that suggests that fake content often contains
commonsense. Accordingly, we develop commonsense expressions
for articles to highlight potential conﬂicts between the inferred
commonsense triplets and the established ones derived from re-
liable commonsense reasoning tools. According to the used tools,
we induce two variants DEMUC-KLM using the knowledge language
model COMET and DEMUC-LLM using the large language models.
These generated expressions are then applied as augmentations
to each article, enabling any MD method to be trained on these
augmented datasets. Additionally, we have manually compiled
a new dataset CoMis, which consists exclusively of fake articles
characterized by commonsense conﬂicts. By integrating DEMUC
with various existing MD frameworks and evaluating them on four
public benchmark datasets and CoMis, our empirical ﬁndings show
that both DEMUC-KLM and DEMUC-LLM consistently and signif-
icantly outperform current MD baselines, while also generating
precise commonsense expressions.
Index Terms—Social media, misinformation detection, large
language models, commonsense reasoning.

sections.heading: Commonsense Conflicts With LLM Workflows
sections.text: Bing Wang , Graduate Student Member, IEEE , Ximing Li , Changchun Li, Bingrui Zhao , Graduate Student Member, IEEE , Renchu Guan , Senior Member, IEEE , Lin Yuanbo Wu , Senior Member, IEEE , and Jungong Han , Senior Member, IEEE Abstract —The advancement of Internet technology has spurred a rise in the dissemination of misinformation, which has had pro- foundly negative impacts across a wide array of fields. To address this issue, the field of Misinformation Detection (MD), which fo- cuses on the automated identification of online misinformation, has gained significant traction among researchers. In our study, we introduce an innovative plug-and-play augmentation technique for MD, termed DEtecting Misinformation by Uncovering Common- sense Conflict (D EMUC ). Our approach is grounded in previous psy- chological research that suggests that fake content often contains commonsense. Accordingly, we develop commonsense expressions for articles to highlight potential conflicts between the inferred commonsense triplets and the established ones derived from re- liable commonsense reasoning tools. According to the used tools, we induce two variants D EMUC - KLM using the knowledge language model COMET and D EMUC - LLM using the large language models. These generated expressions are then applied as augmentations to each article, enabling any MD method to be trained on these augmented datasets. Additionally, we have manually compiled a new dataset CoMis , which consists exclusively of fake articles characterized by commonsense conflicts. By integrating D EMUC with various existing MD frameworks and evaluating them on four public benchmark datasets and CoMis , our empirical findings show that both D EMUC - KLM and D EMUC - LLM consistently and signif- icantly outperform current MD baselines, while also generating precise commonsense expressions. Index Terms —Social media, misinformation detection, large language models, commonsense reasoning. Received 28 May 2025; revised 30 November 2025; accepted 26 December 2025. To address the challenge of identifying misinformation through the simulation of human-like reasoning regarding com- monsenseconflicts,acriticalissueishowtoquantifyandexpress such conflicts within given articles. To this end, we introduce an innovative plug-and-play augmentation approach for the MD task, namely DE tecting M isinformation by U ncovering C ommonsense C onflict ( D EMUC ). Specifically, our method fo- cuses on recognizing and expressing commonsense conflicts as textual descriptions to augment the original article. However, we have observed that current deep learning models, including large-scale LLMs, struggle to accurately identify these con- flicts in a single step, as the experimental findings detailed in Section II . Fortunately, we also discover that LLMs have the capability to accurately perform information extraction, such as identifying check-worthy commonsense elements in articles. This observation inspires us to decompose the identification of the commonsense conflicts as multiple sub-steps, which can be effectively addressed using recent LLM workflows [18] . To implement this, we propose measuring the commonsense conflicts in articles by comparing the extracted commonsense triplets with the golden triplets generated by established com- monsense reasoning tools, such as COMET [19] , [20] and LLMs [21] , [22] . These triplets are then used to populate a predefined commonsense template to create commonsense ex- pressions that express the potential commonsense conflicts. For each article, we combine it with its corresponding specific commonsense expression to produce an augmented version, referred to as a commonsense-augmented article . With these augmented articles, one can develop effective detectors using any existing MD methods and backbones. According to the used languagemodelsinthisprocess,weinducetwovariants D EMUC - KLM with knowledge-enhanced language models, e.g., COMET, and D EMUC - LLM with large language models, e.g., Qwen3 [22] . To conduct our empirical evaluations, we utilize four pub- licly available benchmark datasets GossipCop [23] , Weibo [5] , PolitiFact [23] and Snopes [24] . Furthermore, we have manually compiled a novel dataset, the C ommonsense- o riented

sections.text: information benchmark, referred to as CoMis . This new dataset is characterized by the fact that all of its fake articles are rooted in commonsense conflict. We integrate D EMUC with a variety of established MD frameworks and evaluate their per- formance across both the public benchmark datasets and CoMis . The empirical findings reveal that D EMUC consistently surpasses the performance of existing MD baselines. Our source code and data are released in https://github.com/wangbing1416/MD- PCC. The primary contributions of this paper can be summarized as the following three-folds: r We observe that humans identify misinformation by identifying commonsense conflicts within articles. To simulate this process, we propose a plug-and-play en- hanced MD framework named D EMUC , and induce two variants D EMUC - KLM and D EMUC - LLM that lever- age knowledge-based language models and LLMs, respectively. r To fully evaluate the performance of D EMUC , we collect a new commonsense-oriented MD dataset, named CoMis , in which all articles can be verified using commonsense knowledge, and all fake articles are caused by common- sense conflicts. r We conduct experiments on four publicly available MD datasets and our constructed dataset CoMis , demonstrating that our method D EMUC not only improves the performance of baseline models but also effectively identifies common- sense conflicts within articles. Remark: This paper is an extension version of our previous conference paper [25] . This paper extends our earlier work in several important aspects: 1) In the previous version, we solely employed COMET for identifying commonsense conflicts. With the advance- ment of LLMs, we evaluate their performance in detect- ing such conflicts in this extended version. Specifically, we experimentally reveal that LLMs, particularly the 7B parameter models, struggle to directly identify common- sense conflicts in articles, but they excel at extracting commonsense elements. (Section II ); 2) To enhance the ability of LLMs to recognize common- sense conflicts, we design a series of LLM workflows as alternatives and introduce a new variant D EMUC - LLM for detecting misinformation. A. LLMs are Bad Veracity Predictors First, we investigate the suitability of LLMs for predicting the veracity of articles. Previous studies have provided prelimi- nary conclusions [13] , [26] , [27] , indicating that LLMs perform poorly in detecting misinformation on social media. In this sec- tion, we further evaluate the performance of LLMs in predicting veracity labels and leveraging their inherent knowledge on our constructed knowledge-intensive dataset CoMis (see its details in Section IV ). Specifically, we evaluate the performance of two LLMs Qwen and DeepSeek , and two supervised MD models BERT and CED on the CoMis dataset, respectively. We report their prediction accuracy and confusion matrices in Fig. 1 . For two LLMs, we prompt them using the following template: This is a piece of news content. Please analyze its veracity based on factual knowledge and only output ”real” or ”fake” without adding any explanations, processes or other content. [Article]

sections.text: significantly underperform in veracity prediction compared to supervised models . For example, Qwen and DeepSeek achieve accuracy rates of only 67% and 52%, respectively, and their predictions exhibit a clear tendency to classify fake articles as real. This not only underscores that LLMs struggle to predict the veracity labels accurately but also highlights their diffi- culty in detecting subtle cues of misinformation, leading them to misclassify fake information as real. Additionally, Table II presents several examples of Qwen ’s veracity predictions and their corresponding rationales. In the second and third examples, the LLM provides incorrect veracity predictions. This further illustrates that LLMs often fail to identify the key elements that determine an article’s veracity and, in some cases, even generate rationales that contain factual errors. B. LLMs are Bad Conflict Identifiers In this section, we evaluate the capability of LLMs to directly identify commonsense conflicts within articles. Similarly, we conduct these evaluations using our constructed CoMis dataset, in which all articles can be verified through commonsense knowledge. This characteristic of this dataset enables us to directly evaluate whether models are capable of identifying commonsense conflicts based on its accuracy on this dataset. We also employ the two LLMs for evaluation and report their accuracy and confusion matrices in Fig. 1 . The prompt templates for the two LLMs are as follows: This is a news content. Please determine whether the news is inconsistent with the currently known real-world commonsense knowledge and only output ”inconsistency” or ”consistency” without adding any explanation, process or other content. sections.heading: Generally, LLMs struggle to directly identify potential
sections.text: commonsense conflicts within articles. For example, the ac- curacy rates of Qwen and DeepSeek in detecting such conflicts are only 58% and 51%, respectively, which are even lower than their performance in directly predicting the veracity labels of the articles. Some representative cases in Table II further illustrate that LLMs often fail to detect critical commonsense conflicts within articles, and may even generate significant factual errors by erroneously accepting misleading knowledge due to contex- tual influences. The phenomenon that LLMs tend to be misled by context, or in other words, their weak belief in the correctness of their own answers, has also been confirmed by the current community [28] , [29] . C. LLMs are Good Extractors Although LLMs encounter challenges in directly predicting theveracitylabelsandidentifyingcommonsenseconflictswithin articles, our findings indicate that they do possess the ca- pability to identify check-worthy commonsense elements . This suggests that LLMs can disentangle sub-claims that require validation, even though they face difficulties in directly verify- ing these claims. To illustrate this observation, we select 200 samples from the CoMis dataset, which includes 100 factually accurate articles and 100 fake articles that contain commonsense conflicts. We then employ the following prompt to instruct the LLMs to extract the sub-claims that require verification: This is news piece. Please determine whether the news contains the following relations: 1. A is made of B, 2. A is located in B, 3. A is B, 4. A is a part of B, 5. B exists in A, 6.

Formally, given a fake article x f containing a com- monsense conflict in a triplet ( s , r, o ) , the LLM is considered successful if it correctly extracts that conflict triplet. For a correct article x r with no commonsense conflict, the extraction is deemed successful only if the model produces triplets that are largely accurate—without errors, redundancy, or omissions. For example, in Case ➊ in Table II , DeepSeek failed to ex- tract the triplet correctly and is therefore considered failed. In another example in Table II , we present a case where the article states the fake claim: ” Appropriate exercise promotes the excretion of toxins in the body .” The LLM successfully extracts the underlying commonsense element ” Sweat contains toxins ,” which can be independently verified to demonstrate that the original article is fake. Therefore, in Fig. 2 , we present the success scores from our manual evaluation. The experimental results indicate that Qwen and DeepSeek accurately extract these verifiable commonsense elements in 78% and 73% of the sam- ples, respectively. Compared to their ability to directly identify commonsense conflicts, this suggests that LLMs are relatively more capable of extracting such elements for further verification. Preliminaries Task definition of MD: The primary objective of MD is to develop a misinformation detector, denoted as F θ ( · ) , using a provided training dataset D . This detector F θ ( · ) is then em- ployed to classify unseen articles as either real or fake. Formally, thetrainingdataset D = { x i , y i } N i =1 consistsof N samples,each comprising an unprocessed article x i and its associated veracity label y i ∈{ 0 , 1 } , where 0 signifies a fake article and 1 indicates a real one. The training process for any specific detector F θ ( · ) involves minimizing the following loss function with respect to the parameters θ : min θ L ( θ ) = 1 N N � i =1 ℓ BCE ( F θ ( x i ) , y i ) , (1) where ℓ BCE ( · , · ) represents the binary cross-entropy loss, a standard choice in such classification tasks. Commonsense reasoning methods: In current commonsense reasoning methods, the focus is on training an LM using the relation triplet ( s , r, o ) , where s and o represent the subject and object, and r denotes their relationship. These methods are designed to predict the object o when provided with a subject-relation pair ( s , r ) . Typically, such models are trained on the ATOMIC 20 20 dataset [20] , which contains a number of relation triplets. The relations in ATOMIC 20 20 , which are oriented towards commonsense, include { xNeed , xAttr , xReact , xEffect , xWant , xIntent , oEffect , oReact , oWant , isAfter , HasSubEvent , HinderedBy }. These relations pertain to the interactions between specific events or human actions. Addi- tionally, these methods can be extended to a more extensive knowledge base, ConceptNet [30] , to encompass relationships { MadeOf , AtLocation , isA , Partof , HasA , UsedFor }, thereby capturing the connections between a broader range of entities. For simplicity, we denote the set of these relations as R . In this paper, we implement the commonsense reasoning with a knowledge language model and an LLM, and induce D EMUC - KLM and D EMUC - LLM . B. Overview of D EMUC Our basic idea draws on the premise that fake articles are more prone to contain commonsense conflicts. Meanwhile, our experimental results in Section II also reveal that LLMs struggle with identifying commonsense conflicts but excel at extracting commonsense elements. Accordingly, these insights lead us to propose a plug-and-play augmentation method for the MD task named D EMUC . Specifically, D EMUC develops a commonsense template to express potential commonsense conflicts, as quan- tified by widely used commonsense reasoning methods. This template is then tailored to each original article as part of the augmentation process. Specifically, the commonsense template is structured to: c ⊕ s ⊕ Γ( r ) ⊕ ˆo [ ⊕ “ insteadof ′′ ⊕ o ] , where ( s , r, o ) represents the representative commonsense triplet derived from the original article, ˆo is the golded object associated with ( s , r ) , generated through commonsense reason- ing techniques. The term Γ( r ) refers to the natural language expression of the relation r ; for example, ”is made of” is the original form of the relation MadeOf . We formulate that a commonsenseconflictwithinanarticleisidentifiedwhen o ̸ = ˆo . Conversely, if o = ˆo , no conflict is present. Accordingly, to explicitly express the conflicts, we use the adversative con- junction ”However” to introduce c when a conflict exists (i.e., o ̸ = ˆo ). In contrast, the D EMUC - KLM variant utilizes a smaller LLM, T5 [34] , since unlike the D EMUC - LLM variant, D EMUC - KLM cannot reuse this LLM in subsequent stages. Therefore, we utilize a more lightweight model. Additionally, due to the strong reasoning capability of the LLM in the D EMUC - LLM variant, we can further enhance the efficiency of triplet extraction through grouped inference. Specifically, instead of performing inference for each relation in R individually, we conduct simultaneous inference for ap- proximately six relations , 1 as demonstrated in the prompt used in Section II-C . Moreover, leveraging the general-purpose capability of LLMs, we introduce a new open relation category Other , for the D EMUC - LLM variant. This allows the model to extract triplets corresponding to relations that are not included in the predefined set R . Because not all relations in R are always relevant within an article, we implement a filtering mechanism to eliminate those that lack significance. This filtering approach is grounded in the conditional generation logits, following the principle that generative models typically assign lower probabilities to words they are less certain about. This uncertainty can be quantified using perplexity [35] , [36] . More specifically, we formulate the text generated by G Φ ( · ) in (4) as t γ i = { t γ i 1 , t γ i 2 , . . . , t γ iL } , where L represents the length of the text. Our Collected CoMis To verify whether our method can accurately capture com- monsense conflicts in articles, we collect a new commonsense- oriented MD dataset, denoted as CoMis , with the assistance of human annotators. Table V presents the statistical details of this dataset. The CoMis encompasses 1,580 articles, spanning a wide array of domains, with food safety being the most extensively covered area. Table VI illustrates several representative exam- ples from CoMis , where the original Chinese content has been translated into English. The verification of these instances can be achieved through the application of commonsense knowledge. For example, Example ➌ can be broken down into a common- sense triplet: {PersonX beats mosquito corpses, xEffect , Per- sonX has a fungal infection}. sections.text: O UR B ENCHMARK D ATASET C O M IS First, we carefully choose appropriate data entries from estab- lished datasets that are specified for disclosing fake news and rumors, e.g., Weibo-16 , Weibo-20 , and Weibo-COVID19 . Specif- ically, Weibo-16 [3] includes posts from December 2010 to April 2014, with many duplicates being meticulously removed by [4] . Weibo-20 [4] expands the time frame of Weibo-16 , covering data from April 2014 to November 2018. The labels in this dataset have been validated using a fact-checking platform NewsVerify (https://www.newsverify.com/); Weibo-COVID19 [39] is gath- ered during the peak of the COVID-19 pandemic, and all articles in this dataset are exclusively focused on topics related to COVID-19. To ensure the comprehensiveness and timeliness, we have also manually gathered commonsense-oriented examples from two external Chinese websites. The first source is Food Rumor (http://www.xinhuanet.com/food/sppy/), a platform dedicated to debunking misinformation, with a primary focus on food safety, health science, and related areas. The second source is Science Facts (https://piyao.kepuchina.cn/) which specializes in the dissemination of science popularization content, covering a wide range of topics including food safety, disease prevention and treatment, and biological science. The dataset’s sources and their respective sample counts are detailed in Table VII . It is worth noting that the two external websites, Science Facts and Food Rumor , are both dedicated to debunking misinformation, which leads to a significant predominance of fake claims over real ones. For entries originating from estab- lished MD datasets, we preserve their original veracity labels to ensure consistency with prior benchmarks. Then, these entries undergo a systematic preprocessing stage in which extraneous symbols, such as non-alphanumeric special characters, and any embedded URLs are removed to standardize the text format and eliminate potential noise. For data collected from external online platforms, we adopt a targeted sampling strategy: fake items are sourced from the rumor-debunking sections of reputable fact-checking portals, where each article has been previously verified by domain experts, while real items are obtained from science communication and educational sections of authoritative websites. This length normalization minimizes potential bias stemming from text size variation and facilitates fairer evaluation. V. Implementation details: In our experimental settings of D EMUC - KLM , we utilize the pre-trained language models FlanT5 Large [43] and mT5 Large [44] to extract commonsense triplets from the English and Chinese MD datasets, respectively. For generating golden objects, we employ COMET-ATOMIC 20 20 [20] for English datasets and comet-atomic-zh for Chinese datasets, specifically Weibo and CoMis . During the training phase, we apply an Adam optimizer with a learning rate of 7 × 10 − 5 for the BERT model in the baseline methods. For other components, such as the linear classifier, we set the learning rate to 1 × 10 − 4 . The batch size is maintained at 64 throughout the training. Additionally, we empirically determine and fix certain parameters, setting K , ϵ , and μ to 5, 0.8, and 0.6, respectively. To prevent overfitting, we implement an early stopping strategy, which halts the training process if no improvement in the Macro F1 score is observed over 10 consecutive epochs. Additional data processing and analysis methods [45] , [46] can also be referred for use. Evaluation metrics: Let TP , TN , FP , FN denote true posi- tives, true negatives, false positives, and false negatives, respec- tively. For the MD task that contains “real” and “fake” classes, Accuracy = T P + T N T P + T N + F P + F N measures the overall correct- ness of the binary detector; Macro F1 = 1 2 ( 2 · T P 2 · T P + F P + F N + 2 · T N 2 · T N + F N + F P ) is the unweighted average of the F1-scores com- puted for each class independently; Precision = 1 2 ( T P T P + F P + T N T N + F N ) measures how many of the predicted positives are cor- rect; Finally, Recall = 1 2 ( T P T P + F N + T N T N + F P ) measures how many of the actual positives were correctly identified. B. Main Results Tables VIII and IX present the performance outcomes of our method, D EMUC , on four benchmark datasets and our con- structed dataset CoMis . To minimize the impact of randomness, each experiment was conducted five times with different random seeds: {1, 2, 3, 4, 5}. The standard deviations from these five trials are also provided in Tables VIII and IX . Generally, our D EMUC method,whichservesasaplug-inapproach,consistently and significantly enhances the performance of baseline models across all evaluation metrics. For instance, on the Weibo dataset, D EMUC improves the overall F1 score by 1.91 and the fake news F1 score by 2.54 compared to the state-of-the-art MD method, CED. Similarly, on the GossipCop dataset, D EMUC achieves improvements of 1.46 and 3.19 in macro F1 and preci- sion scores, respectively. When comparing the performance of D EMUC across different MD datasets, we find that it generally outperforms on CoMis compared to the other Chinese dataset, Weibo , across most metrics. Specifically, relative to the BERT baseline, D EMUC enhances the macro F1 and precision scores by 1.16 and 0.74 on Weibo , while it demonstrates more substantial improvements of 2.85 and 2.52 on CoMis . These findings under- score the effectiveness of D EMUC in leveraging commonsense knowledge to improve the detection of misinformation rich in contextual information. C. Ablative Study To evaluate the efficacy of the critical components within D EMUC - KLM , we perform a series of ablation studies. These experiments are carried out on four benchmark MD datasets, and we introduce three ablative versions of CED + D EMUC - KLM as follows: D EMUC - KLM without ICL : This variant omits the ICL component (with K = 0 ) during the commonsense triplet extraction phase; D EMUC - KLM without c : This version excludes conjunction words such as ”However” in the formulation of commonsense expressions; D EMUC - KLM without o : This iter- ation removes the phrase ”instead of” along with o from the commonsense expressions. E. Sensitivity Analysis

sections.heading: Number of in-context examples
sections.text: K . In Section V-C , the quantity of in-context examples, denoted as K , is a crucial factor in determining the effectiveness of extracting commonsense triplets. To further explore this, we conduct a sensitivity analysis by varying K within the set {1, 3, 5, 7, 9}. The empirical findings from this analysis are illustrated in Fig. 5 . The experiments are conducted across all four MD baseline models using the Gos- sipCop dataset. Our results show that D EMUC attains its highest F1 score when K is set to either 3 or 5. Additionally, the data consistently demonstrate a decline in performance as K deviates from these optimal values, whether increasing or decreasing. In some cases, the model’s performance even falls below that of the baseline model without D EMUC . This suggests that an inadequate selection of K can lead to suboptimal extraction of commonsense triplets, thereby introducing noise and negatively impacting overall model performance.

The detailed training and infer- ence (generating commonsense expressions) time and memory costs are shown in Table XII . Specifically, it takes approximately 5 minutes to train a misinformation detector F θ ( · ) , and 6 hours per 10,000 articles to generate commonsense expressions. Since the parameters of our used T5 model and COMET are frozen, the generating process only consumes approximately 7G memory. VI. R ELATED W ORKS In this section, we briefly review the related literature about misinformation detection and commonsense reasoning. A. Misinformation Detection Misinformation, such as fake news and rumors, has had a profoundly negative impact on society [1] , [47] . Consequently, the identification and detection of misinformation, a field known as misinformation detection, has become increasingly crucial. SOTA MD techniques primarily focus on identifying misinfor- mation by analyzing its textual and multimodal content, employ- ing sophisticated deep learning models [3] , [48] , [49] , [50] , [51] , e.g., Transformers [52] , sentence embeddings [53] , [54] and their parameter-efficient methods [55] . These models frequently integrate external features, including emotional cues [4] , user feedback [3] , [56] , and temporal evolution [57] , [58] . In addition to detecting misinformation based solely on textual content, some studies have also explored leveraging auxiliary information such as information propagation networks in social media for improved detection [23] , [56] , [61] , [62] . Building upon such social networks, subsequent modeling of information spread and the mitigation of misinformation are also critical aspects [63] , [64] . In this study, we incorporate commonsense knowledge into MDmodels.PriorstudieshaveattemptedtoenhanceMDmodels by utilizing knowledge graphs. These efforts mainly focus on learning knowledge embeddings [10] , [65] or retrieving entity descriptions [11] , [66] . Unlike these previous approaches, our method of integrating commonsense knowledge is more aligned with human reasoning and natural responses. B. Commonsense Bases and Reasoning Commonsense knowledge bases, including Concept Net [30] and ATOMIC 20 20 [20] , serve as invaluable resources for direct commonsensereasoning.Theyhavebeenappliedinawiderange of academic fields, such as machine translation [67] , question answering [68] , and sarcasm detection [69] . Recently, the in- tegration of commonsense reasoning with LLMs has attracted considerable interest [67] , [70] , [71] . These studies often use commonsense knowledge as additional information or evaluate the extent to which LLMs incorporate such knowledge. In addi- tion to this, a related task in the NLP community has focused on evaluating the factuality and factual consistency of text gener- ated by LLMs [72] , [73] . However, these evaluations primarily follow the natural language inference framework and assess the semantic similarity between the generated text and reference gold standards, without explicit comparison to commonsense knowledge bases.

sections.heading: ONCLUSION AND
sections.text: D ISCUSSION In this paper, we aim to enhance MD models by uncovering commonsense conflicts. To achieve this goal, we propose a novel MD method named D EMUC , designed to generate commonsense expressions for each article, explicitly expressing commonsense conflict existing inherent in articles, and leverage it to aug- ment original articles. Specifically, the expression is constructed through a commonsense triplet extracted from the original arti- cle, the corresponding golden object, and a conjunction word. To obtain these components, we first prompt the pre-trained language model with in-context examples to extract triplets and filter out irrelevant triplets. Then, the commonsense tool is employed to generate their corresponding golden objects. Finally, a new metric is designed to measure the commonsense conflict, and the conjunction word is determined using this met- ric. Discussion and future works: In this paper, we aim to sim- ulate the human process of identifying commonsense con- flicts in misinformation. Our experiments reveal that even SOTA LLMs cannot directly and accurately detect such con- flicts. To address this limitation, we propose a workflow- based method leveraging language models. Looking ahead, as LLMs continue to improve and eventually become capa- ble of recognizing commonsense inconsistencies, the next key step will be exploring how to elicit their knowledge recalling abilities through a single prompt.
